items.title: 13.2.3 Nature of Excretory Products in relation to Habitat

source_refs.note: Topic 13.2.3 with the uric acid box (PDF 6-7).

blocks.text: In many animals osmoregulation is linked with removing nitrogenous wastes, which are excreted dissolved in water. The form of waste depends on how much water the habitat allows.

blocks.caption: Nitrogenous wastes
rows: Ammonia (NH3): formed in the liver when amino groups removed from amino acids and nucleic acids combine with H+
highly toxic; about 500 mL of water per gram
ammonotelic: most fishes, protozoans, sponges, coelenterates; marine animals release it straight into the water
Urea, CO(NH2)2: made from ammonia in the liver
less toxic; about 50 mL per gram
Uric acid, C5H4N4O3: made from ammonia using much energy; forms precipitates
least toxic and less soluble; about 1 mL per gram
uricotelic: insects, desert animals, birds, most reptiles

blocks.text: Humans also excrete a little uric acid, a by-product of breaking down purines from foods such as meat. When there is too much uric acid in the blood, crystals can form in joints and tissues, causing the painful condition called gout.

blocks.alt: Top left: a freshwater fish with water arrows entering, a large volume of dilute urine leaving and salts taken in by active transport. Top right: a marine bony fish with water arrows leaving, sea water drunk, little concentrated urine and chloride cells pumping salts out. Bottom left: ammonia, urea and uric acid with about 500, 50 and 1 mL of water per gram as bars. Bottom right: human responses to overheating and to cooling.
blocks.caption: Osmoregulation, nitrogenous wastes and human thermoregulation (original diagram after topics 13.2 and 13.3).
blocks.long_description: A freshwater fish is saltier than the water around it, so water keeps entering by osmosis and salts leak out; it produces a large volume of dilute urine and takes salts back in by active transport, and rarely drinks. A marine bony fish is less salty than sea water, so it loses water and gains salt; it drinks sea water, makes little concentrated urine and uses chloride cells in its gills to pump salt out. Ammonia needs about 500 mL of water per gram to excrete safely, urea about 50 mL and uric acid about 1 mL, so animals short of water excrete urea or uric acid. When the human body is too hot, skin vessels widen and sweat cools it; when it is too cold, skin vessels narrow, muscles shiver and hairs stand up.
